# Account Planning for the Top Twenty

Source: https://lowob.com/research/account-planning-for-the-top-twenty/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-15 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Key account programmes underperform with unusual consistency: Gartner found 58% of B2B sales organisations missing quota on key accounts and most rebuilding their programmes repeatedly. The causes are selection by size of spend, plans that are written once, and coordination that stops at the sales team. This piece sets out a selection rule, a one-page plan, a monthly review and the record that makes each plan a set of decisions rather than a document.

Account planning for the top twenty is the discipline of choosing the twenty or so customers with the most room to grow, writing a short plan for each, and reviewing those plans monthly with the people who serve the account. The evidence says most firms get the selection wrong and the cadence wrong. Gartner found customers chosen as key accounts mainly for their large spend were 51% less likely to increase it, and that organisations which update plans frequently and use them in customer decisions are three times more likely to build the customer's decision confidence. Pick by potential, keep the plan to a page, and review it every month.

*Figure: The wiring turns nine places into one brief. It cannot retrieve a decision nobody wrote down; that is the record's job.*

Most firms of 20 to 500 people know who their largest customers are. Fewer have decided which customers deserve a plan, and fewer still keep those plans current after the first quarter. The result is familiar: a set of documents written during annual planning, read once in a review, and consulted again a year later.

[*What is account planning?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-account-planning/) covers the definition and the contents of a plan. This piece covers how to run planning for a defined set of accounts as a routine: how to choose them, how short the plan should be, and how the monthly review turns it into decisions.

## Why key account programmes keep being rebuilt

Gartner's research on key accounts, reported in 2021, is unusually blunt. In a survey of 69 chief sales officers, 95% expected higher growth from key accounts than from other customers. Yet 58% of B2B sales organisations missed quota on those accounts, and 46% had rebuilt their key account programme two or more times in seven years because it underperformed. Gartner's current summary puts the share that have rebuilt at least once in seven years at 79%.

Gartner's diagnosis, as reported by CRM Magazine, is a sales-centric view: key accounts are chosen and managed by the sales team, when what they need is a commitment from the wider firm. The supporting figure is that key account managers reporting high cross-functional collaboration saw roughly three times higher spend from key customers, while 66% of key account managers say internal coordination limits their ability to plan.

Academic research reaches a similar conclusion from a different direction. Homburg, Workman and Jensen's cross-industry, cross-national study in the Journal of Marketing identified eight distinct ways firms organise key account management and found significant performance differences between them, which suggests the design of the routine matters as much as the effort put into it.

That points to three failures, and the rest of this piece addresses them in order: the wrong accounts, a plan nobody uses, and a review that includes only sellers.

## Choosing the twenty

Twenty is a working number, not a rule. It is about as many plans as a revenue leader can review in depth each month, and in most mid-size firms it covers a large share of revenue. A firm of 30 people may have eight; a firm of 300 may have forty split across two leaders.

The selection should weigh growth potential and the firm's ability to capture it, which Gartner calls opportunity alignment. Size of current spend is one input, not the criterion.

| Criterion | What to look at | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Headroom | Estimated total spend in your category minus what you already have | The account must have room to grow |
| Fit | How closely the account matches your ideal customer profile | Growth is cheaper where you already deliver well |
| Relationship breadth | Number of senior contacts and functions you serve | Single-threaded accounts are fragile |
| Strategic intent | Whether the customer is investing in the problem you solve | Budget follows priorities |
| Health | Delivery satisfaction, usage, open issues | You cannot expand an unhappy account |
| Current spend | Revenue in the last twelve months | Protects what matters today, but should not decide alone |

Score each candidate on a simple scale and choose the top twenty, then check the list against revenue concentration. If the list leaves out an account that represents a large share of revenue, protect it with a retention plan rather than a growth plan. [*How to write an ICP*](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-write-an-icp/) covers how to define fit so it can be scored consistently.

Re-tier twice a year. Gartner's own recommendation is to monitor relationship health and move accounts out of the programme when they stop performing, rather than overinvesting in them.

## The one-page plan

A plan that runs to twenty slides will not be read monthly. A plan that fits on one page will.

| Section | Contents | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The customer's goal | What the customer is trying to achieve this year, in their words | Account lead |
| Where we help | The two or three places your work connects to that goal | Account lead |
| Decision map | Who decides, who influences, who is sceptical, and how well you know each | Account lead and delivery lead |
| Objectives | Two to four objectives, each with a measure and a date | Account lead |
| Actions | The next action for each objective, with an owner from any function | Named owners |
| Risks | What could lose the account or stall growth | Account lead and delivery lead |
| Last review | Date, what changed, what was decided | Account lead |

Two features matter more than the rest. The customer's goal comes first, so the plan starts from the customer's agenda rather than your product list. And actions can be owned by anyone, including delivery, finance or a partner, which is how the plan carries the cross-functional coordination that Gartner found so often missing.

The plan also inherits from earlier parts of this series. The decision map and risks start from the handover pack described in Part 27. Renewal dates and expansion targets connect to Part 24. Each objective is, in effect, a commercial decision, and should be recorded as one.

> An account plan is a set of decisions about one customer. If none of them has an owner and a date, it is a description.

## The monthly review

The review is where plans either stay alive or quietly die. Gartner reports that organisations which update account plans frequently, and rely on them to guide customer decisions, are three times more likely to build customer decision confidence, and that customers with high decision confidence are ten times more likely to make a high-quality, low-regret purchase.

CRM vendors say the same about the document itself. Salesforce's training module on account plans calls the plan "a living document" and says "This isn't a one-time exercise", but sets no review schedule, which is the gap a monthly cadence fills. Its suggested contents (an account vision, the customer's priorities and success metrics, and the competitive landscape) map onto the one-page plan above.

A monthly review for twenty accounts can be done in under two hours if it is disciplined.

**Review by exception.** Each account lead reports only what changed: an objective's status, a new risk, a stakeholder change. Accounts with no change take thirty seconds.

**Include delivery.** The delivery lead for each account attends, or sends a written note. That is where health issues surface before they reach the renewal.

**Decide, then record.** Each review should produce decisions: pursue an opportunity, add a senior sponsor, pause expansion until an issue is fixed. Each decision gets an owner and a check date in the record.

**Update the page in the meeting.** The plan's "last review" line is updated before the meeting ends. A plan that is updated afterwards usually is not.

McKinsey's 2024 B2B Pulse survey of nearly 4,000 decision makers found buyers using an average of ten interaction channels, up from five in 2016, and suggested that large, important accounts may benefit from a dedicated representative plus self-service. For the top twenty, the review is where that coverage is set: who owns each relationship, and which channels the customer actually uses.

## Why the effort pays

The economic case for account planning rests on retention and expansion rather than new logos. Fred Reichheld's work at Bain found that in financial services a 5% increase in customer retention produced more than a 25% increase in profit. The figure is old and sector-specific, and it is often stretched beyond what it says. The mechanism holds more widely: retained customers cost less to serve and buy more over time.

For recurring-revenue firms the same logic shows in net revenue retention. SaaS Capital's 2025 benchmarks put median net revenue retention at 102% for private companies with annual contract values of $25,000 to $50,000, and found groups with retention of 110% or more grew faster than the median. Expansion has to come from somewhere, and account planning concentrates effort on the customers with the most headroom rather than spreading it evenly.

| Programme health signal | Healthy | Warning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plans reviewed in the last month | All twenty | Fewer than fifteen |
| Objectives with an owner and a date | All | Some with neither |
| Actions owned outside sales | Several per plan | None |
| Accounts re-tiered in the last six months | Some moved in and out | List unchanged for a year |
| Decisions recorded from reviews | Several a month | None |

## The plan as a record

An account plan is one of the clearest cases of a commercial record that a firm already writes and then fails to keep. The objectives are decisions. The review is where their status is updated. The outcome, expansion or retention, arrives within a year.

That makes it a natural place for the record and the context layer to meet. The figure above shows the problem: an account's history sits across inboxes, call recordings, proposal versions and memory. The context layer can assemble the brief before each review. It cannot supply the reason the firm chose to pursue one opportunity and not another. That is the account lead's job, written in the plan.

Illustrative example: moving an account out of the twenty

Decision
:   Move the second-largest account from the growth programme to a retention plan, and add a smaller account with more headroom.

Reason and owner
:   The account had little category spend left to win and a single senior contact; the replacement scored higher on headroom and strategic intent. Owned by the revenue lead, agreed with the chief executive.

What changed
:   The large account keeps a quarterly retention review with its delivery lead. The new account gets a full plan and a named executive sponsor; both are checked at the next re-tiering.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B technology firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Select by potential, not spend.** Large current spend predicts less growth than most firms expect.
- **Keep the plan to one page.** The customer's goal first, then objectives with owners and dates.
- **Review monthly, with delivery in the room.** Report by exception and decide before the meeting ends.
- **Record each objective as a decision.** Owner, status and check date turn a plan into evidence.

Gateway card

### Before you call it a key account programme

- A written selection rule weighing headroom, fit and health as well as spend
- One-page plans for every account on the list
- At least one action per plan owned outside sales
- A monthly review with delivery represented
- Decisions from each review recorded with an owner and a check date
- A re-tiering date in the calendar, twice a year
